title: Fitting a tile edge trim strip to an exposed tile cut
subtitle: Bed a metal or plastic tile trim into the adhesive at the edge of a tiled surface to give a clean, finished edge on a cut tile
excerpt: How to fit a tile edge trim strip where a tiled surface ends at an exposed cut edge. Covers choosing the right trim profile, setting the trim in tile adhesive, and grouting the joint.
sourceNotes: Collins Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced). UK tile trade practice and tiling specification guides (open access).

glossaryTerms.definition: A metal or plastic profile strip that is bedded into tile adhesive at the edge of a tiled area to protect and finish the cut edges of tiles. Common profiles: square-edge trim, round-edge trim (schluter), and angle trim for external corners. Available in stainless steel, chrome-plated steel, aluminium, and PVC.

content.text: covers the rough cut face of a tile where the tiled surface stops at a doorway, a window reveal, or a change of plane. The trim is set in tile adhesive at the same time as the last tile in the row. Fitting it as you tile (not afterwards) gives the cleanest result.

The trim height must match the tile thickness. A 10 mm tile needs a 10 mm trim. The most common profiles are the round-edge trim (the wing closes over the cut edge and covers it entirely) and the square-edge trim (the wing sits proud of the tile face and is visible as a metal or plastic strip). Round-edge trim is cleaner; square-edge is easier to apply. For a wet area such as a shower, use stainless steel or anodised aluminium rather than chrome-plated mild steel.

Apply tile adhesive to the wall or floor in the usual way. Press the trim into the adhesive with the perforated wing embedded and the profile face projecting at the tile face level. The perforations key into the adhesive. Check that the trim is flush with the top face of the tiles; any variation shows at the grout joint. Immediately press the last full tile alongside the trim, embedding both in the adhesive at the same time. The tile should sit snugly against the upright section of the trim with a grout gap of 2-3 mm.

Allow the adhesive to set fully before grouting. Apply grout into the gap between the tile and the trim with a grout float or a filling knife, pressing it firmly into the joint. Wipe excess off the trim face with a damp sponge before the grout dries. A grout of the same colour as the tiles gives a clean finish; a contrasting grout can look good but draws attention to any variation in the joint width.

Cut the trim with tin snips or a fine-tooth tenon saw. For mitred internal corners (a shower recess, for example), cut both pieces at 45 degrees with the mitre saw. Clean up any burr on the cut end with a fine file. The butt joint at a corner is less neat than a mitre but is acceptable in most situations.

attrs.symptom: The trim sits proud of the tile face after grouting
attrs.cause: The trim was not pressed fully into the adhesive at the same depth as the tiles, or the trim height does not match the tile thickness.
attrs.fix: If the adhesive is still green, remove and re-bed the trim at the correct depth. If set, use a fine grinder or trim saw to reduce the projecting edge.

attrs.symptom: Grout falls out of the joint at the trim within a few months
attrs.cause: Movement at the tile edge; a rigid grout cracks at a joint where two different materials meet.
attrs.fix: Rake out the failed grout and replace with a colour-matched flexible silicone sealant, which accommodates the slight differential movement.
